key_terms.meaning: One instrument that combines an electronic theodolite, an EDM and a processor, so it measures horizontal angle, vertical angle and slope distance and computes coordinates at a single setup.

Distance from the phase difference between a transmitted and returned modulated signal: d = (φ/2π) × (λ/2) + nλ/2, where λ is the modulation wavelength in metres and n is the whole number of half-wavelengths.
A fixed offset, typically 0 mm or −30 mm, added to the measured distance to correct for the light path inside the prism and its mounting.
A sensor that measures the small tilt of the instrument in two directions and corrects the measured horizontal and vertical angles for it.
A setup method in which the instrument occupies an unknown point and computes its own coordinates from angles and distances measured to two or more known points.
Global Navigation Satellite System: any satellite constellation broadcasting ranging signals, such as GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou and NavIC.
Range found as ρ = c × Δt, where c = 2.998 × 10⁸ m/s is the speed of light and Δt is the signal travel time in seconds; it carries clock and atmospheric bias.
The data stream broadcast by each satellite at 50 bit/s giving its ephemeris, clock correction, almanac and health status.
The tracked count of whole and fractional cycles of the L1 carrier at 1575.42 MHz; used for centimetre-level relative positioning.
Real-Time Kinematic: carrier-phase positioning corrected in real time by a base station or network over a radio or internet link, giving a few centimetres of horizontal accuracy.
A dimensionless number describing satellite geometry, such that position error σ<sub>p</sub> = DOP × σ<sub>range</sub>.
The lowest elevation above the horizon, commonly 10° to 15°, at which a receiver will accept a satellite's signals.
Light Detection and Ranging: range from the two-way travel time of a laser pulse, R = c × t ÷ 2, with c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s and t in seconds.
A dense set of points with x, y, z coordinates, often with intensity or colour, that describes a scanned surface.
The ground size of one image pixel: GSD = (pixel size × flying height) ÷ focal length, both lengths in the same unit.
The fraction of a photograph that reappears in the next one along the flight line or in the next strip; drone mapping uses about 70 % to 80 % forward and 60 % to 70 % side overlap.
A method that matches features in many overlapping photographs and solves camera positions and 3D point coordinates together.
Marking on the ground the plan position, level and alignment of a designed point by bearing and distance from known control.
Measurement of water depth and bed shape, usually by sound: depth = (v × t) ÷ 2, where v ≈ 1500 m/s in sea water and t is the echo time in seconds.
A transducer that sends a sound pulse downwards and times its return, giving depth under the vessel after correcting for transducer draft and sound speed.

takeaways: A total station is one instrument that measures angle and distance and turns them into coordinates, but only after prism constant, atmospheric correction and two-face collimation checks are applied.
GNSS position comes from travel time: range = c × time, and four unknowns (x, y, z and receiver clock) need four satellites.
Code pseudorange gives metre-level accuracy; carrier-phase RTK gives centimetre-level accuracy but needs a base station or correction service within about 10–20 km.
DOP converts range error into position error, so good satellite spread and a clear sky matter more than the price of the receiver.
LiDAR ranges directly by laser time of flight and produces a dense 3D point cloud day or night, limited by timing resolution, scan angle and the GNSS/IMU solution.
Drone mapping is photogrammetry at scale: planned overlap plus known camera positions plus SfM produce an orthomosaic and a surface or terrain model whose detail is fixed by the GSD.
Setting out reverses surveying: compute bearing and distance from control to the design point, guide the operator to it, then check by an independent method.
Under water and underground the same control logic applies, but sound replaces light and plumb wires or gyros replace line of sight.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to join the working principle, a labelled sketch, a named list of error sources with magnitudes and units, and a field procedure or accuracy check, with the numerical or comparison part carrying most of the marks.

Distance: modulated infrared beam, phase comparison gives slope distance; corrections for prism constant, atmospheric temperature and pressure, and earth curvature and refraction

answer.text: Components and their jobs.

head: Part
What it does
rows: Tribrach with foot screws, circular bubble and laser or optical plummet
levels the instrument and centres it over the station mark
Horizontal and vertical circles with encoders
read angles electronically, typically to 1″ to 5″
measures the remaining tilt of the vertical axis and corrects the angles
sends a modulated infrared beam to the prism and measures the slope distance S from the phase of the return
applies corrections, reduces S, computes coordinates, runs programs (stake-out, resection, area)
stores raw and reduced data; USB or Bluetooth to the office
returns the beam; its prism constant k is entered with its sign

answer: Principle of the EDM. The beam is modulated at a known wavelength λ. The phase difference between the outgoing and returning signal gives the part of a wavelength in the double path; several modulation frequencies (coarse and fine) give the whole number. Two-way path 2S = nλ + Δλ, so S = (nλ + Δλ)/2.

Step 1, set up. Centre and level over P, measure the instrument height HI, enter the station coordinates (E, N, RL), the prism constant, and the air temperature and pressure for the atmospheric correction (about 1 ppm per °C; a 10 °C error is 10 ppm, 1.2 mm on 120 m).
Step 2, orient. Sight the backsight Q and set the horizontal circle to its azimuth (here 30°00′00″). From now on the circle reads azimuths.

answer.text: Step 3, measure and reduce. Sight the prism at R: the instrument reads the horizontal circle, the zenith angle z and the slope distance S, then corrects S for the prism constant and the atmosphere before reducing it.
Step 4, coordinates and level.

answer: Step 5, store and check. The point is stored with its code. Before leaving, a known point is measured again; its coordinates must repeat within the job tolerance, which proves that the orientation did not move.
Onboard programs. Stake-out (the reverse computation), resection from two or more known points, remote elevation, offsets, missing line, area and volume.

Order of the corrections. The processor corrects the slope distance before it reduces it: prism constant first, then the atmospheric (ppm) correction, then, on long sights, curvature and refraction. A reading of 120.030 m with a −30 mm prism becomes 120.000 m; an atmospheric correction of +8 ppm then adds 120 × 8 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.001 m.

Why it replaced the theodolite and tape. Angle and distance are measured together on one line of sight, in seconds, with no taping over rough ground; the reductions are done without arithmetic slips; the data are stored for the office; and the same instrument sets out points by the reverse computation.
Check. √(115.196² + 31.947²) = √(13 270.1 + 1020.6) = √14 290.7 = 119.543 m, the horizontal distance, so the coordinate differences are consistent with d.

bank.q: Explain the principle of GNSS positioning. Distinguish code and carrier measurements, and list the absolute and relative positioning methods.
outline: Satellites act as moving known points; broadcast ephemeris gives their position at the time of transmission
Travel time gives pseudorange; three ranges fix x, y, z, a fourth satellite removes the receiver clock error
Position by trilateration and least squares
Navigation message carries ephemeris, clock terms, almanac and health
Segments: space, control, user
Methods: single point (a few metres), DGPS (about 1 m), RTK or network RTK (about 2 cm), static carrier-phase processing (millimetres) for control
answer: Principle. Each satellite is a moving point whose position at the time of transmission is known from its broadcast ephemeris. The receiver measures the travel time of the signal and turns it into a range; ranges from several satellites fix the receiver by trilateration.

answer.text: The range equation. The receiver clock is cheap and not synchronised, so each measured range is a pseudorange:
answer.pre:
ρ<sub>i</sub> = √((X<sub>i</sub> − x)² + (Y<sub>i</sub> − y)² + (Z<sub>i</sub> − z)²) + c δt
unknowns x, y, z and δt  →  at least four satellites

answer.text: Worked range. Satellite at (15 000 000, 10 000 000, 20 000 000) m, receiver at (6 378 137, 0, 0) m, clock 1.000 ms ahead.

answer: Segments. Space segment (the satellites and their clocks and signals), control segment (monitor stations, master control, upload of orbits and clock corrections) and user segment (receivers and antennas).

answer.text: Code and carrier measurements.

head: Item
Code pseudorange
Carrier phase
rows: time shift of a known code
unknown whole number of cycles N

answer: Absolute positioning. One receiver alone (single-point positioning, SPP) with code ranges and the broadcast orbits: a few metres, limited by orbit, clock and atmospheric errors. Precise point positioning (PPP) uses precise orbits and clocks with carrier phase to reach centimetres after a long convergence.

answer.text: Relative positioning. A base on a known point and a rover share the same errors, which cancel in the difference.

head: Method
Data
Typical accuracy
rows: carrier phase, ambiguities fixed in the field
1 to 3 cm, base within about 10 to 20 km
carrier phase from a CORS network
carrier phase logged for an hour or more, processed later

answer: Why four and not three. Three spheres meet at a point only if the clock is perfect; the fourth satellite gives the fourth equation for δt. A 1 ms error is 299 792 m of range, so the clock term cannot be ignored.

answer.text: Errors and what relative positioning does to them.

head: Error
Size in SPP
In DGPS or RTK over a short baseline
rows: mostly cancels; dual frequency removes the rest
up to a few metres at low elevation
mostly cancels; models for height differences
does not cancel: site and antenna choice

answer: Check. ρ − r = 24 265 111 − 23 965 319 = 299 792 m = c × 0.001 s, the clock term only, as it should be.

bank.q: What is DOP? Explain GDOP, PDOP, HDOP and VDOP, and show how satellite geometry affects the accuracy of a GNSS position.
outline: Define DOP from the geometry matrix; σ<sub>position</sub> = DOP × σ<sub>range</sub>
Satellites spread widely in the sky give low DOP; satellites bunched together give high DOP
GDOP includes position and time; PDOP is 3D position; HDOP horizontal; VDOP vertical, usually the largest
Typical values: PDOP below 4 is good, above 8 is poor
Mask angle, obstruction, urban canyon and tree canopy raise DOP
Mission planning software predicts DOP before the survey
answer: Definition. Dilution of precision is the factor by which the geometry of the satellites multiplies the range error into a position error: σposition = DOP × σrange. It depends only on the directions to the satellites, not on the signals.

answer.text: From the geometry matrix. Each satellite gives a row of H: minus the unit vector from receiver to satellite (east, north, up components) and 1 for the clock. With Q = (HᵀH)⁻¹:
answer.pre:
GDOP = √(q<sub>EE</sub> + q<sub>NN</sub> + q<sub>UU</sub> + q<sub>TT</sub>)   position and time
PDOP = √(q<sub>EE</sub> + q<sub>NN</sub> + q<sub>UU</sub>)          3D position
HDOP = √(q<sub>EE</sub> + q<sub>NN</sub>)                 horizontal
VDOP = √q<sub>UU</sub>                          vertical
TDOP = √q<sub>TT</sub>                          clock

answer.text: A worked geometry. One satellite at the zenith and three at 30° elevation, at azimuths 0°, 120° and 240°, against four bunched satellites at azimuths 0°, 20°, 340° and 10° and elevations 20°, 40°, 30° and 60° (Q computed by inverting HᵀH):

answer: Reading the table. The same four satellites give a forty-fold worse fix when bunched: the rows of H are nearly alike, HᵀH is nearly singular and its inverse is large. VDOP exceeds HDOP even in the good sky because every satellite is above the horizon, so height and clock are hard to separate.

answer.text: Effect on accuracy. With σrange = 3.0 m:
answer.pre:
spread:  horizontal 1.33 × 3.0 = 4.0 m,  vertical 2.31 × 3.0 = 6.9 m
bunched: horizontal 39.3 × 3.0 = 118 m,  vertical 34.0 × 3.0 = 102 m

answer: The simplest case. In two dimensions with unit vectors (0, 1) and (1, 0), HᵀH = I and HDOP = √2 = 1.414; with both satellites along (0, 1), HᵀH = [[0, 0], [0, 2]] is singular and HDOP is infinite.

In practice. PDOP below about 4 is good and above about 8 is poor. Planning software predicts DOP for the day; obstructions, a high mask angle, urban canyons and canopy raise it; adding a fifth satellite at 10° elevation and azimuth 60° to the spread sky lowers PDOP from 2.67 to 2.25.
What DOP does not do. It scales random range noise; it does not remove multipath, atmospheric delay or a wrong antenna height. A low DOP with a biased range still gives a wrong fix.

Mask angle in numbers. In the spread sky with the fifth satellite at 10° elevation, a 10° mask keeps it and PDOP is 2.25; raising the mask to 15° rejects it and PDOP returns to 2.67. A higher mask cuts low-elevation noise but costs geometry.
Check. For the spread sky, PDOP² = HDOP² + VDOP²: 1.333² + 2.309² = 1.778 + 5.333 = 7.111 = 2.667², and GDOP² = PDOP² + TDOP² = 7.111 + 2.333 = 9.444 = 3.073².

bank.q: Explain the principle of LiDAR and describe airborne, terrestrial and mobile LiDAR with their components and typical accuracies.
outline: Range from two-way laser time of flight, R = c × t ÷ 2; scanning mirror spreads pulses into a swath
Components: laser, scanner, GNSS, IMU, camera, data recorder
Airborne: 500 m to 3000 m above ground, 5 cm to 30 cm vertical accuracy, multiple returns
Terrestrial static scanner: millimetre accuracy over 100 m to 1000 m range
Mobile mapping on a vehicle: survey-grade point cloud of road corridors
Products: DEM, DSM, canopy and ground separation, 3D city models, volume and corridor mapping; works at night, cloud and vegetation limits

answer.text: Principle. A laser sends a short pulse; the timer measures the two-way travel time t to the surface and back.
answer.pre:
R = c t / 2
t = 2.00 µs:  R = 299 792 458 × 2.00 × 10⁻⁶ / 2 = 299.792 m
a timing error of 1 ns is a range error of c × 10⁻⁹ / 2 = 0.15 m

answer: Components. Laser (near-infrared on land, green for shallow water), scanning mirror that steers the pulses, detector and timer, GNSS receiver for position, IMU for roll, pitch and heading, and a recorder. Each point = sensor position + range along the known beam direction, with an intensity value.

answer.text: Airborne LiDAR. On an aircraft or helicopter, scanning across the flight line. Example: H = 1000 m, scan ±20°, 200 000 pulses per second, 60 m/s.
answer.pre:
swath = 2 × 1000 × tan 20° = 727.9 m
density = 200 000 / (60 × 727.9) = 4.58 points per m²

answer: Returns. One pulse can give several returns: the first from the canopy (digital surface model) and the last from the ground through gaps in the leaves (digital terrain model after classification). This is why LiDAR maps the ground under forest where photogrammetry cannot.

Terrestrial LiDAR (TLS). A scanner on a tripod turns about its vertical axis and sweeps the beam vertically, recording millions of points from tens to hundreds of metres. Scans from several set-ups are joined on targets or on overlapping surfaces. Used for building façades, rock slopes, tunnels, heritage structures and industrial plant.

Mobile LiDAR. Scanners on a vehicle with GNSS and IMU record road and rail corridors at traffic speed. Accuracy depends on the GNSS/IMU trajectory, so control points along the route are used to adjust it, particularly under bridges and between tall buildings.

answer.text: Typical accuracies.

head: Platform
Range
Typical accuracy
Main limit
rows: up to a few hundred m
a few mm at tens of metres

answer.text: Why attitude matters. An angular error θ moves a point sideways by R θ:

answer: Products and checks. Classified point cloud, DTM and DSM, canopy height (DSM − DTM), contours, building models, power-line clearances. Every product is checked against ground control points measured by GNSS or total station.

LiDAR against photogrammetry. LiDAR measures each range directly, needs no texture or daylight and reaches the ground through gaps in vegetation; photogrammetry needs overlapping images of a textured, lit surface but gives colour and an orthomosaic. Many drone and aircraft systems now carry both.
Check. 200 000 points per second over 60 × 727.9 = 43 676 m² per second gives 4.58 per m², and the average spacing 1/√4.58 = 0.47 m.

bank.q: Describe a complete drone survey: mission planning, overlap and GSD, ground control, processing by structure from motion, and the products obtained.
outline: Define area, required accuracy and output; compute flying height for the target GSD
Flight planning: strip design, 70 % to 80 % forward overlap, 60 % to 70 % side overlap, constant height, camera trigger interval
Payload: RGB, multispectral or LiDAR; ground control points or RTK/PPK positioning
Image matching by SfM, bundle adjustment, dense matching
Products: orthomosaic, DSM, DEM, contour map, 3D model, volume
Accuracy check against checkpoints; DGCA drone rules and permissions in India
answer: 1. Reconnaissance and permissions. Inspect the site for obstacles, take-off areas and the ground cover; check the airspace zone and permissions; choose a multirotor for a small site or close work, a fixed-wing or VTOL for long strips.

answer.text: 2. Mission planning: GSD. Choose the flying height from the detail needed. With p = 2.4 µm and f = 8.8 mm:
3. Overlap and flight lines. At 120 m an image of 5472 × 3648 pixels (short side along track) covers 119.4 m × 179.1 m. For a 3.0 km × 0.5 km corridor:
answer.pre:
forward overlap 80 %:  119.4 × 0.20 = 23.9 m between photos  → 126 intervals, 127 images per strip
side overlap 70 %:     179.1 × 0.30 = 53.7 m between strips
strips = ⌈(500 − 179.1) / 53.7⌉ + 1 = 6 + 1 = 7  → 7 × 127 = 889 images
flight line 7 × 3000 = 21 km at 10 m/s = 35 min, plus turns; a photo every 23.9/10 = 2.4 s

answer: 4. Ground control. Mark ground control points (GCPs) with targets several GSD across, spread round the edge and through the middle, and measure them by RTK GNSS or total station. Keep extra marked points as independent checkpoints that are not used in processing. With RTK or PPK camera positions, fewer GCPs are needed, but a few are kept to catch datum and height errors.

5. Flight. Fly the planned lines at constant height above ground, with shutter speed fast enough to avoid blur (motion during exposure well under one GSD), in even light and low wind, within visual line of sight.

6. Processing by structure from motion. Detect keypoints in every image; match them in overlapping images; solve the camera calibration, camera positions and tie points together by bundle adjustment, using the GCPs to fix scale, position and orientation; build the dense cloud; classify ground and non-ground points.

answer.text: 7. Products.

head: Product
What it is
Typical use
rows: seamless, scale-true image map at about one GSD

answer.text: 8. Accuracy check. Compare checkpoint heights from the model with their surveyed values. Residuals of +0.03, −0.05, +0.04, −0.02 and +0.06 m give

Common faults and their causes. Blurred images (shutter too slow for the speed), gaps in matching over water, sand or uniform crops (no texture), a "bowl" distortion of the DSM (poor camera calibration, no GCPs in the middle), and wrong heights from a datum mismatch between the GCPs and the RTK camera positions. At 10 m/s with a 1/1000 s shutter the drone moves
answer.pre: 10 × 0.001 = 0.010 m = 0.31 GSD at 3.27 cm  (acceptable; aim for under 0.5 GSD)

answer: Report. State the camera, flying height and GSD, overlaps, number and layout of GCPs and checkpoints, datum and geoid model, processing software, checkpoint RMSE in plan and height, and the date of flight.
Check. 0.042 m is 1.3 GSD at 3.27 cm, within the usual expectation of about 1 to 3 GSD vertically for a well-controlled block, so the model can be accepted for a 1:500 plan with 0.25 m contours.

answer: Step 4: field procedure. Set up over A with forced centring, enter the coordinates of A and B (or zero the circle on B), and check the distance AB = √(100² + 50²) = 111.803 m by measuring it. For each point, turn β, guide the prism along the line until the distance agrees, drive a peg and mark the exact point with a nail. With a stake-out program the display shows the remaining left/right and in/out values directly.

Step 5: checks on the building itself. Measure the sides (30.000 and 20.000 m) and both diagonals, which must be equal: √(30² + 20²) = 36.056 m. Re-measure every peg from B, or resect from a third control point. Unequal diagonals show a rotated or shifted corner even when the sides are right.

Step 6: transfer to profile boards. Pegs at corners are lost when the foundation is dug, so the grid lines are extended 2 to 3 m beyond the corners onto profile boards (or offset pegs) at a set level, and string lines between nails on the boards give the lines again during construction.
Levels. The top of each peg or board is set from a benchmark with a level: if the design level is 101.250 m and the height of instrument is 101.385 m, the staff must read 0.135 m on the peg.

answer.text: Expected accuracy. With angles to 5″ and distances to 2 mm + 2 ppm, the farthest corner P2 is fixed to about
answer.pre:
across the line: 76.158 × 5/206 265 = 1.8 mm
along the line:  2 + 2 × 0.076 = 2.2 mm
together about √(1.8² + 2.2²) = 2.8 mm, inside a typical ±5 mm for building grid lines

answer: Check the control first. Before any peg is set, measure from A the angle between B and a third control point and compare it with the angle computed from their coordinates. A disturbed control mark found now costs minutes; found after the foundations are cast, it costs the building.
Check. From A: P1 at 50.000 m and P2 at 76.158 m with angle 63°26′06″ − 49°45′49″ = 13°40′17″ between them give P1P2 = √(50² + 76.158² − 2 × 50 × 76.158 × cos 13°40′17″) = 30.000 m, the design side.

bank.q: Write the observation equation for one pseudorange and show how four pseudoranges give the receiver position and clock error; explain where DOP enters.
outline: ρ<sub>i</sub> = √((x<sub>i</sub> − x)² + (y<sub>i</sub> − y)² + (z<sub>i</sub> − z)²) + c × δt, with satellite position from ephemeris and δt the receiver clock offset
Four unknowns x, y, z and δt, so four satellites are the minimum
Linearise by Taylor series about an approximate position and solve by least squares
Geometry matrix gives the covariance and hence DOP
Mention ionospheric and tropospheric delay, and how dual frequency or models reduce the ionospheric part
Accuracy statement: single point a few metres; RTK a few centimetres

answer.text: Observation equation. For satellite i at (Xi, Yi, Zi) and a receiver at (x, y, z) with clock bias δt:
answer.pre: ρ<sub>i</sub> = √((X<sub>i</sub> − x)² + (Y<sub>i</sub> − y)² + (Z<sub>i</sub> − z)²) + c δt + ε<sub>i</sub>

answer: The terms. ρi is the measured pseudorange, the root is the geometric range ri, c δt the receiver clock term (the same for all satellites at one epoch), εi the remaining errors (satellite clock and orbit residuals, ionosphere, troposphere, multipath, noise).

answer.text: Linearising. Start from an approximate position (x₀, y₀, z₀) and δt₀ = 0. Expanding about it, with ei the unit vector from the receiver to satellite i:
answer.pre:
Δρ<sub>i</sub> = ρ<sub>i</sub> − r<sub>i0</sub> = −e<sub>xi</sub> Δx − e<sub>yi</sub> Δy − e<sub>zi</sub> Δz + c δt
row i of H = [−e<sub>xi</sub>, −e<sub>yi</sub>, −e<sub>zi</sub>, 1]

answer.text: Four satellites. Four equations in four unknowns:
answer.pre:
Δρ = H Δu,   Δu = (Δx, Δy, Δz, c δt)
with exactly four: Δu = H⁻¹ Δρ
with more than four (least squares): Δu = (HᵀH)⁻¹ Hᵀ Δρ
update x₀ ← x₀ + Δx ..., recompute r<sub>i0</sub>, repeat until Δu is negligible (usually 3 or 4 passes)

answer.text: A numerical test of the clock column. Suppose the approximate position is exactly right but the clock is 1.000 ms ahead. Then every Δρi = 299 792 m, and the solution must be:
answer.pre:
Δρ = (299 792, 299 792, 299 792, 299 792)
Δu = (0, 0, 0, 299 792): position unchanged, c δt = 299 792 m, δt = 1.000 ms
because the fourth column of H is all ones, a common shift is taken wholly by the clock

answer.text: Where DOP enters. If every pseudorange has the same independent error σ, the covariance of the solution is
answer.pre:
Σ<sub>u</sub> = σ² (HᵀH)⁻¹ = σ² Q
GDOP = √trace Q,  PDOP = √(q<sub>11</sub> + q<sub>22</sub> + q<sub>33</sub>),  TDOP = √q<sub>44</sub>
(with H rotated into east, north, up: HDOP = √(q<sub>EE</sub> + q<sub>NN</sub>), VDOP = √q<sub>UU</sub>)

answer.text: Numbers for one sky. Zenith plus three satellites at 30° elevation, 120° apart in azimuth:

answer: Why the geometry matters. The up and clock columns of H are coupled (the −2.5 term), because every satellite is above the horizon: raising the antenna and advancing the clock both shorten all the ranges. That coupling makes VDOP larger than HDOP.

answer.text: The full equation. Written out, the error term contains:
answer.pre:
ρ<sub>i</sub> = r<sub>i</sub> + c (δt − δt<sup>s</sup>) + I<sub>i</sub> + T<sub>i</sub> + M<sub>i</sub> + e<sub>i</sub>
δt<sup>s</sup>: satellite clock, from the navigation message
I<sub>i</sub>: ionosphere, from a model or removed by two frequencies
T<sub>i</sub>: troposphere, from a model
M<sub>i</sub>, e<sub>i</sub>: multipath and noise, left in the residuals

answer: Corrections before solving. The satellite clock and the models are applied to ρi first; only the receiver position and clock are solved. With more than four satellites the residuals ρ − Hu show whether one range is bad, which is how a receiver flags multipath or a faulty satellite.
Check. The east–north block of HᵀH is diagonal with 1.125 = 3 × cos²30° / 2 = 3 × 0.75/2, so qEE = qNN = 1/1.125 = 0.889 and HDOP = √1.778 = 1.33, matching the table.

bank.q: Describe the procedure for a hydrographic survey of a reservoir, from horizontal control to the plotting of the bed contour map.
outline: Horizontal control along the bank by total station traverse or GNSS; mark ranges or use DGPS/RTK on the boat
Vertical control: gauge or tide staff, water level at the time of sounding
Echo sounder with transducer draft, bar check before and after the survey, sound velocity correction
Line spacing and run lines; record time, position and depth for each sounding
Reduce soundings to chart datum: reduced level = water level − depth
Plot soundings, draw bed contours, compute capacity by cross sections or by a surface model; list errors
answer: 1. Horizontal control. Fix control stations round the reservoir by GNSS (static or RTK from a CORS) or by a traverse, with marks on stable ground and in sight of the water. They are used to set up a shore total station, to check the boat GNSS, and to fix the ends of the sounding lines.

2. Vertical control and water level. Run levels from a benchmark to a staff gauge in the water. The water level (RL of the surface) is read at intervals during the survey, or logged by an automatic gauge, because every depth must be reduced to a level.

3. Sounding plan. Lay out parallel sounding lines across the reservoir at a spacing set by the scale of the map and the roughness of the bed (closer near dam, intakes and old river channels), with a few cross lines to check. Near the banks, where the boat cannot go, the ground is surveyed by total station or GNSS on foot.

answer.text: 4. Calibrating the echo sounder. A bar check: a plate lowered to a known depth below the transducer. If the bar is at 5.00 m and the sounder reads 5.06 m, the sound speed set is too high:
answer.pre:
true c = 1500 × 5.00 / 5.06 = 1482.2 m/s
set 1482 m/s, or measure a sound velocity profile

answer: 5. Sounding and position fixing. The boat runs each line at steady speed. Each sounding is stored with its position (RTK GNSS on the transducer pole, or a shore total station tracking a prism on the boat) and the time, so that the water level at that moment can be applied.

answer.text: 6. Reduction. Depth below the surface = sounder depth + transducer draft; bed RL = water level − depth below the surface.
answer.pre:
water level 245.60 m, sounder 12.00 m, draft 0.40 m
depth below surface = 12.00 + 0.40 = 12.40 m
bed RL = 245.60 − 12.40 = 233.20 m

answer: 7. Plotting the bed contour map. Plot the reduced bed levels at their positions with the shoreline and control; interpolate contours (for example every 2 m) by hand or by a TIN in software; check where sounding lines cross; mark the dam, intake and spillway.

answer.text: 8. Capacity. Areas inside contours are measured (planimeter or software). With 1.20 ha at 234 m, 1.85 ha at 236 m and 2.60 ha at 238 m:

answer: 9. Report. State the datum, the water levels used, the sounder calibration, the checks at crossing lines and the capacity table, so a later survey can be compared to measure siltation.

Equipment. A stable boat with a transducer pole, a single-beam or multibeam echo sounder, a bar or sound-velocity probe, RTK GNSS (or a shore total station with a prism on the boat), a staff gauge or water-level logger, levelling equipment for the gauge, and a laptop logging position, depth and time together.

Check. Crossing lines should agree within the stated tolerance; for example a 0.12 m disagreement at a crossing in 12 m of water is 1 %, comparable with the 1.2 % sound-speed error that the bar check removed.

bank.q: For a topographic survey of a 200 hectare site you may use a total station, RTK GNSS or a drone. Compare the three for accuracy, production rate, cost and checking, and recommend one with reasons.
outline: Accuracy: total station 5 mm to 10 mm at the point, RTK about 20 mm to 30 mm horizontal, drone 20 mm to 50 mm with control points
Production: total station about 200 to 500 points a day, RTK 500 to 1500 points a day, drone 200 ha in a couple of hours of flying
Cost in rupees: capital, daily hire, processing software, and manpower
Limitation: total station needs line of sight and a helper, RTK fails under canopy, drone needs open sky and permission
Checks: known baseline for total station, repeated point and DOP for RTK, independent checkpoints for the drone
Recommend a drone flight with GNSS control points, with total station used for hidden and boundary detail
answer: The job. 200 ha = 2 000 000 m². A plan at 1:1000 with 0.5 m contours needs heights on about a 20 m grid plus breaklines and detail: 2 000 000/400 = 5000 grid points, and more along roads, drains and buildings.

answer.text: Accuracy.

head: Method
Plan
Height
Notes
rows: needs line of sight and a traverse frame
needs open sky; each point independent
GSD 2.73 cm at 100 m with the chapter camera; poor under trees

answer.text: Production rate (typical, open ground). Taking about 400 points a day by total station and 800 by RTK:
answer.pre:
total station: 5000 / 400 = 12.5 crew-days, plus the traverse
RTK GNSS:      5000 / 800 = 6.3 crew-days
drone at 120 m: 53.7 m strip spacing × 10 m/s × 25 min = 15 km of line ≈ 80.5 ha per flight
               200 / 80.5 = 2.5 → 3 flights, about one field day plus GCPs

answer: Cost. The total station is cheapest to own but slowest; RTK needs a base or a CORS subscription; the drone needs the aircraft, a trained remote pilot, permissions and processing software, but the field cost per hectare is the lowest and the product (orthomosaic, DSM, DTM) is the richest.

Checking. Total station: closed traverses and check points. RTK: re-occupy known points twice a day and at different satellite geometry. Drone: independent checkpoints not used in the processing, and RMSE reported.

answer.text: Comparison.

answer: Recommendation. Use the drone for the bulk of a 200 ha site, controlled by GCPs fixed by RTK GNSS (or static GNSS tied to the national datum). Use RTK to pick up checkpoints and open-ground breaklines, and a total station for wooded parts, building corners, culverts and any area where GNSS is blocked.

Why. The drone covers the area in a day at a vertical accuracy of a few centimetres, which suits 0.5 m contours; RTK and the total station fill exactly the places the drone cannot see and give the independent check.
Check. 1 to 3 GSD at 2.73 cm is 2.7 to 8.2 cm, well inside a quarter of the 0.5 m contour interval (0.125 m), so the drone product meets the plan specification on open ground.

bank.q: Compare the error sources and the final accuracy of a total station closed traverse with an RTK GNSS control survey, and state which method should control the other and why.
outline: Total station errors: angular seconds accumulate with distance, EDM scale and atmospheric error parts per million, centering and target height
GNSS errors: orbit and clock, ionosphere, troposphere, multipath, DOP, antenna phase centre
Error propagation: traverse misclosure in mm against distance; GNSS relative accuracy of 10 mm + 1 ppm
Angular control must come from GNSS or a known azimuth because a traverse drifts in orientation
Total station is better in canopy, near structures and for short hidden lines
Practice: GNSS fixes the control points, total station fills detail and sets out; check both against a common baseline

answer.text: Total station traverse: error sources.

head: Source
Effect
rows: swing every later leg; errors accumulate along the traverse
Distance errors (2 mm + 2 ppm, prism constant, atmosphere)

answer.text: Final accuracy of the traverse. A 2 km traverse of ten 200 m legs closing at 1 in 20 000 has a closing error of 2000/20 000 = 0.10 m. After Bowditch adjustment the middle stations are the weakest, because their error is the largest share of the accumulated misclosure.
answer.pre:
leg 200 m with 2 mm + 2 ppm: 2 + 0.4 = 2.4 mm
angle error 3″ swings the next station 200 × 3/206 265 = 2.9 mm

answer.text: RTK GNSS control: error sources.

head: Source
Effect
rows: scales all errors; worse in the vertical
a base error shifts every point; ppm grows with distance
Wrong ambiguity fix, wrong antenna height

answer: Final accuracy of RTK. About 1 to 2 cm in plan and 2 to 4 cm in height per point, independent of the distance between points, with no accumulation along a route. Static GNSS on long sessions reaches a few millimetres plus about 0.5 ppm.

answer.text: Relative accuracy over short and long distances.
answer.pre:
two RTK points 50 m apart, 15 mm each: √2 × 15 = 21 mm between them
two total station points 50 m apart from one set-up: about 2 to 3 mm
two points 2 km apart: RTK about 21 mm; traverse up to 100 mm before adjustment

answer: Which controls which. Over a large area the GNSS (preferably static, tied to the national datum) controls the total station: it fixes the frame with no build-up of error, and the traverse is run between pairs of GNSS points so that its misclosure is measured and adjusted. Over a small site with short distances, the total station gives the better relative accuracy, so it carries the detail and setting out from the GNSS-fixed frame.

Checking each against the other. A traverse between two GNSS pairs gives an independent check of both; a total station distance between two GNSS points checks the GNSS scale; repeat RTK at a different time checks multipath and ambiguity.
Conclusion. GNSS for the network (no accumulation, absolute datum), total station for local density and short-range precision, each checked by the other.

Heights. A total station gives trigonometric height differences, close to levelled ones over short sights. GNSS gives ellipsoidal heights; to compare them with levelled heights the geoid undulation N must be applied (H = h − N), and a change in N of 0.3 m across a site shows up directly as a height error if it is ignored. For height control, levelling or the total station controls GNSS.
Check. The traverse misclosure of 0.10 m on 2 km is about five times the 21 mm RTK relative error, consistent with using GNSS to control the long distances.

bank.q: Evaluate drone photogrammetry for computing earthwork volume of a road embankment against total station cross sections. Discuss GSD, surface extraction, vegetation and the acceptable tolerance.
outline: GSD at 100 m flying height with a 10 mm pixel and 8 mm lens is about 3 cm, so surface detail is at that order
Surface from SfM gives a dense point cloud but follows vegetation and can hide ground under canopy
Total station cross sections are sparse but accurate at the points measured
Volume error depends mainly on the ground model and the formation level, not on point density alone
Cross-check on a known test patch; a few per cent is realistic
Decide against the specification, usually 5 % for earthwork, and use the same datum and boundary for all methods
answer: The job. A road embankment 500 m long with an average cross-section of about 30 m², so about 500 × 30 = 15 000 m³, with a top area of about 500 × 12 = 6000 m².

answer.text: Total station cross sections. Sections every 20 m, each a set of points across the bank; volumes by average end area or the prismoidal formula. For two sections 28.0 and 32.0 m², 20 m apart, with 29.8 m² midway:

answer: Strength and weakness of sections. Each point is accurate to millimetres, but the ground between sections is assumed to vary smoothly; a hump or hollow between two sections is missed, and the result depends on the section interval.

answer.text: Drone surface. Every pixel gives a height: at GSD 2.73 cm (100 m flying height) the surface is sampled about every 3 cm, so humps between sections are captured. Volume = Σ (surface − base) × cell area. Random height errors largely cancel over many cells; a systematic error does not:
answer.pre:
bias 0.03 m over the top area: 6000 × 0.03 = 180 m³
as a share of 15 000 m³: 180/15 000 = 1.2 %

answer: Surface extraction. The DSM includes everything the camera sees. The DTM needs classification to remove vehicles, stockpiled material, equipment and grass; tall grass of 10 cm over the bank would add 6000 × 0.10 = 600 m³ (4 %) if not removed. Fresh, bare earthworks are the best case for drone volumes; vegetated or wet slopes are the worst.

Control and GSD. Accuracy depends on GCPs round and along the embankment, fixed by RTK or total station, and on checkpoints to measure the vertical RMSE. A vertical error of 1 to 3 GSD (2.7 to 8.2 cm here) is typical; the systematic part must be shown small by checkpoints.

Acceptable tolerance. Earthwork payments commonly accept a difference of a few per cent between methods. A 1.2 % bias meets that; 4 % from uncleaned grass does not. The tolerance and the checking method should be agreed before the survey.

answer.text: Evaluation.

head: Criterion
Total station sections
Drone photogrammetry
rows: staff on the bank near plant

answer: Verdict. For a bare embankment with good control, drone volumes are as reliable as cross sections and capture the surface better; for vegetated slopes or final measurement of a contract, keep total station sections, or use them to check the drone surface at a few chainages.

Field procedure for the drone method. Place GCPs at the toe on both sides every 100 to 150 m and checkpoints between them; fly two cross strips as well as the main lines so that the long, narrow block does not bend; survey the base surface (original ground) by the same method before filling, so that both surfaces share the same control.

Check. The two section formulas differ by 600.0 − 597.3 = 2.7 m³ in 600 m³ (0.45 %), smaller than the 1.2 % drone bias, so the method error of the sections is not the deciding factor; the drone bias is.

bank.q: Explain how horizontal control and azimuth are transferred underground through a vertical shaft, and analyse the errors and the checks used in tunnel surveying.
outline: Two plumb wires hung in the shaft, coordinates transferred by joining them to surface control, geometry of the triangle made as flat as possible
Azimuth transfer by gyro-theodolite, or by two shafts with a connecting traverse underground
Level transfer by tape and water level or by a deep staff
Errors: wire swing, refraction and air current in the shaft, small angle at the wires, gyro drift
Checks: closing the traverse between two shafts, comparing gyro and computed azimuth, repeat measurements on different days
Tolerance for tunnel breakthrough and the need for frequent check surveys
answer: The problem. A tunnel driven from a shaft must follow the surface coordinate system, but the shaft gives only a short base for direction. A small azimuth error at the bottom swings the whole tunnel line.
1. Surface control. Fix control at the shaft collar by GNSS or a traverse, with a well-defined azimuth line to a distant reference.

answer.text: 2. Two-wire (coplaning) method. Hang two plumb wires W1 and W2 across the shaft, as far apart as possible, with heavy bobs damped in oil. At the surface fix their coordinates and the azimuth W1W2; underground, line the theodolite in with the two wires and carry that azimuth into the tunnel.

3. Weisbach triangle. When the instrument cannot be exactly in line, set it at C a little off the line; measure the small angle θ at C between the wires and the distances. The angle at W1 follows by the sine rule; for small angles φ = (b/c) θ:

answer: 4. Gyrotheodolite. A gyroscope in the instrument settles on true north, giving the azimuth of a tunnel line directly, independent of the shaft. It is used to check the wire transfer and to control long tunnels at intervals.

5. Two shafts. Where two shafts are available, a wire in each gives a base hundreds of metres long; the underground traverse between them is fitted to the two surface positions, which fixes direction far better than one short base.

6. Levels. Heights are carried down by a steel tape hung in the shaft (corrected for temperature, tension and its own weight) or by EDM measured vertically to a reflector, from a surface benchmark to an underground benchmark.

answer.text: Errors.
answer.pre:
1 mm error in one wire over a 4.000 m base: 0.001/4.000 rad = 52″
10″ azimuth error at 2000 m: 2000 × 10/206 265 = 0.097 m sideways
wires deflected by air currents and dripping water; plumb bobs swinging

answer: Checks. Repeat the transfer several times and on different days; check by gyrotheodolite; run the underground traverse with forced centring and both faces, as a closed loop where possible; carry independent traverses from two headings and compare at breakthrough; re-observe the azimuth as the tunnel advances.

Breakthrough error. The difference between the two headings when they meet, in line, level and chainage. Its predicted size, from the transfer and traverse errors, must be inside the tolerance before excavation starts.

answer.text: Level transfer, worked. A steel tape reads 58.432 m from the surface benchmark (RL 120.000 m) to the underground benchmark at 30 °C, with the tape standard at 20 °C and α = 11.2 × 10⁻⁶ per °C:
answer.pre:
temperature correction = 58.432 × 11.2 × 10⁻⁶ × 10 = +0.0065 m
corrected length = 58.4385 m
RL underground BM = 120.000 − 58.439 = 61.561 m

answer: Check. At 2000 m, the 52″ from a single 1 mm wire error would give 2000 × 52/206 265 = 0.50 m, five times the 10″ case, which is why the wires are observed many times and checked by gyro.

bank.q: Evaluate the limits of GNSS in an urban site and under tree canopy, and discuss remedies and the regulatory limits on drone surveys in India.
outline: Multipath, signal blockage, high DOP and few satellites in an urban canyon; canopy attenuates and scatters the signal
Remedies: raise mask angle carefully, use multi-constellation and dual frequency, network RTK with a short baseline, total station for shadowed points, ground control points for drone work
Best practice: fix control in open sky and carry it by total station
Drone regulation in India: DGCA rules require registration, a remote pilot certificate, permitted zones and no-fly zones near airports and defence areas
Accuracy statement and check against a known point
State when the survey must be refused or replanned
answer: Urban canyon. Buildings block much of the sky. In a street 20 m wide between 30 m buildings, a receiver in the middle sees across the street only above tan⁻¹(30/10) = 71.6° elevation, so only satellites near the zenith or along the street are visible: few satellites, bunched, and a high DOP, particularly in the across-street direction.

Multipath. Glass and concrete reflect signals; the reflected path is longer, so code ranges can be wrong by metres and carrier phase by centimetres. Non-line-of-sight signals, received only by reflection, are the worst case.
Under tree canopy. Leaves and wet branches weaken and scatter the signal; the receiver loses lock, cycle slips break the carrier phase, and RTK ambiguities fail to fix or fix wrongly.

answer.text: Consequences.

head: Effect
Result
rows: longer time to fix, or no fix
PDOP rises above 6 to 8; height worst
a point decimetres away flagged as fixed

answer: Remedies. Multi-constellation, multi-frequency receivers (GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou, NavIC) for more satellites; plan observation windows by DOP; longer occupations and repeat at a different time; antennas and receivers with multipath rejection; tilt-compensated poles to stand back from walls; offset methods; and above all a total station traverse from GNSS points placed in open spaces (parks, roofs, wide junctions) into the canyon or under the trees.

Checking. Re-occupy points after an hour, when the satellite geometry has changed; reject fixes with high PDOP or that change on re-initialisation; check against a total station distance between two points.

Drones and regulation in India. Under the Drone Rules, 2021, administered by the DGCA through the Digital Sky platform, a drone is registered and gets a unique identification number, and the operator needs a remote pilot certificate (with exemptions for the smallest classes). The airspace map divides the country into green zones (flying up to 120 m, 400 ft, without permission), yellow zones (permission from air traffic control) and red zones (permission from the central government). Drones are classed by weight as nano, micro, small, medium and large.

What the rules mean for a survey. Check the zone before planning; most urban survey sites near airports or sensitive buildings are yellow or red, so permission must be obtained in advance; fly within visual line of sight, below the height limit and not over crowds; keep the flight records. In dense cities the flight may be impossible or limited, so the survey falls back on total station and terrestrial or mobile LiDAR.

Evaluation. GNSS is excellent in open country and for control, but in canyons and under canopy it becomes unreliable without warning; a survey there is controlled by GNSS in the open and completed by total station.

Check. With the 71.6° limit, a satellite at 60° elevation across the street is blocked, but one at 60° along the street axis is visible: the visible sky is a narrow strip, which is why the DOP across the street is poor.

glossary.def: The measurement and charting of water depth and the shape of the water bed.
The measured phase of the satellite carrier wave, tracked in cycles and used for high-precision relative positioning.
The fixed low-water level to which charted depths are reduced; charted depth = depth below the surface − tide height above datum.
Digital Elevation Model, the general name for a grid of elevations; often used for the bare-earth surface (DTM), as distinct from a DSM that includes buildings and trees.
Dilution of Precision, a geometry factor that multiplies range error to give position error.
Digital Terrain Model, a grid of bare-earth elevations after buildings and vegetation are removed.
A device that measures depth by timing a sound pulse sent to the bed and back.
An instrument that measures distance from the phase or travel time of a modulated signal sent to a reflector and back.
A theodolite whose horizontal and vertical circle readings are produced electronically by encoders and shown on a display.
The broadcast orbit parameters that let a receiver compute a satellite's position at a given time.
Any global satellite navigation system that provides position and time from ranging signals, such as GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou or NavIC.
A point on the ground whose coordinates are known and which is identifiable in the images, used to georeference and check a survey.
Ground Sample Distance, the ground dimension represented by one pixel of an image.
The extra signal delay caused by free electrons in the ionosphere, reduced by dual-frequency observation or by a model.
A ranging method that uses laser pulses and their two-way travel time to build a dense three-dimensional point cloud.
The elevation below which a receiver ignores satellites, usually 10° to 15°.
A seamless, geometrically corrected image map made by joining many photographs.
The proportion of one photograph repeated in the adjacent photograph or strip, needed for matching and stereo.
A large set of measured points with three-dimensional coordinates describing a surface or object.
The fixed offset added to a measured distance to allow for the light path inside the reflector assembly.
A range obtained from signal travel time multiplied by the speed of light, biased by clock and atmospheric errors.
Determining the occupied station's coordinates from measurements to known points, used in a free station setup.
Real-Time Kinematic positioning, in which carrier-phase corrections from a base station give centimetre accuracy in the field.
The field operation of fixing on the ground a point or line whose position is already defined on a drawing.
A computer-vision photogrammetric method that recovers camera positions and scene points from many overlapping images.
An integrated electronic theodolite, distance meter and computer that measures angles and distances and computes coordinates.
